title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Multidirectional instability of the shoulder is a complex condition characterized by symptomatic glenohumeral instability in 2 or more directions of motion. The multifactorial etiology encompasses congenital hyperlaxity, repetitive microtrauma, and deficits in neuromuscular control. Because clinical presentation is often vague, timely recognition and management remain challenging. Historically, shoulder instability was categorized using the AMBRI/TUBS framework, which divided cases into atraumatic, multidirectional, bilateral, rehabilitative, and inferior capsular shift versus traumatic, unidirectional, Bankart lesion, and surgical repair. While valuable for teaching, this binary model oversimplified the condition and failed to account for overlapping presentations and neuromuscular contributors to instability. Contemporary understanding instead favors a more individualized, evidence-based approach that integrates mechanical, structural, and neuromuscular factors. Accurate diagnosis relies on careful clinical evaluation supported by selective imaging, particularly magnetic resonance arthrography. Management typically follows a stepwise progression, beginning with targeted physical therapy to restore dynamic stabilization, with surgical options such as arthroscopic pancapsular plication reserved for refractory cases.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This continuing education activity equips participants with a comprehensive understanding of the pathophysiology of multidirectional instability, modern diagnostic strategies, and evidence-based treatment pathways. Learners gain the skills to recognize key clinical features, select appropriate imaging modalities, and design tailored rehabilitation protocols. The course also highlights the importance of interprofessional collaboration, showing how coordinated efforts among physicians, advanced practitioners, physical therapists, radiologists, and surgeons enhance diagnostic accuracy, improve patient safety, and ensure patient-centered care. By promoting a team-based approach, this activity fosters stronger communication, reduces the risk of mismanagement, and supports better functional outcomes for individuals with multidirectional shoulder instability.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Differentiate multidirectional instability from other causes of shoulder pain using key historical features, physical examination findings, and characteristic magnetic resonance arthrography results. Assess the multifactorial etiology of multidirectional instability, including the roles of constitutional hyperlaxity, repetitive microtrauma, and underlying neuromuscular control deficits. Develop a comprehensive, evidence-based treatment plan for patients with multidirectional instability, starting with targeted physical therapy that focuses on neuromuscular reeducation and progressing to appropriate surgical indications. Collaborate with physical therapists to implement and monitor a phased rehabilitation program for multidirectional instability that emphasizes scapular stabilization and neuromuscular control, ensuring clear communication regarding patient progress and readiness for surgical consideration. title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Introduction
content: Multidirectional instability (MDI) of the glenohumeral joint is a complex clinical entity characterized by symptomatic, involuntary subluxation or dislocation in 2 or more directions, typically including an inferior component. [1] The condition, first described by Neer and Foster in 1980, highlights the delicate balance between mobility and stability in the human body's most mobile joint; a sophisticated interplay of static and dynamic stabilizers maintains this balance. [2] The static stabilizers include the bony architecture of the glenoid and humeral head, the glenoid labrum, which deepens the socket, the capsuloligamentous complex, and the negative intra-articular pressure. [3] The dynamic stabilizers consist of the muscles surrounding the shoulder joint, including the rotator cuff, the long head of the biceps tendon, and the periscapular musculature, which maintain stability through active concavity-compression and coordinated neuromuscular control. MDI represents a failure of this integrated system, wherein the humeral head translates beyond the physiologic boundaries of the glenoid, resulting in pain, apprehension, and functional disability. [4]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Introduction
content: Historically, shoulder instability was conceptualized through a dichotomous classification system called TUBS (traumatic, unilateral, Bankart, surgical) and AMBRI (atraumatic, multidirectional, bilateral, rehabilitation, inferior capsular shift). While valuable for introducing the concept of atraumatic instability, this framework is now considered obsolete as it fails to account for the significant clinical heterogeneity and the spectrum of pathology observed in patients with MDI. [5] [6] A substantial portion of patients with MDI have a history of trauma, and many with traumatic instability have underlying ligamentous laxity, blurring the lines of this rigid classification. [6] [7]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Introduction
content: A modern approach, reflecting a more advanced understanding of the condition, emphasizes the underlying etiological factors. [5] [6] A recent systematic review proposed a more clinically relevant "AB classification," which categorizes patients based on the presence or absence of (A) significant trauma and (B) generalized hyperlaxity. [8] This framework acknowledges that MDI is not a single entity but a heterogeneous condition. [5] This moves the clinical focus from a rigid algorithm to a patient-specific diagnosis, which better guides treatment decisions and helps standardize future research. [8] This shift in thinking, from a simple dichotomy to a multifactorial spectrum, is fundamental to the contemporary management of MDI. [9] [10]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Etiology
content: The etiology of MDI can be broadly categorized into 2 primary pathways, which may exist independently or concurrently in a given patient. [4] The first pathway is atraumatic or constitutional, from congenital or developmental factors. [4] This is most commonly associated with generalized ligamentous hyperlaxity, a condition characterized by excessive joint mobility. This hyperlaxity can be a feature of systemic connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, or osteogenesis imperfecta, or it can be part of a benign joint hypermobility syndrome. [11] [12] [13] In these individuals, the collagen that comprises the joint capsule and ligaments is inherently more extensible, leading to a patulous and redundant capsuloligamentous complex that provides insufficient static restraint to the glenohumeral joint.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Etiology
content: The second pathway is acquired, most often resulting from repetitive microtrauma. [14] This is frequently observed in overhead athletes, such as swimmers, baseball pitchers, volleyball players, and gymnasts. [15] Over time, the repetitive, high-demand, end-range motions inherent to these sports gradually stretch the static capsuloligamentous stabilizers. [15] This leads to an acquired, sport-specific capsular laxity that may not be associated with generalized hypermobility. Unlike traumatic unidirectional instability, there is typically no identifiable inciting event; the instability develops insidiously as the static restraints progressively fail. [3]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Etiology
content: Regardless of the initial cause, be it a congenitally lax capsule or stretched by repetitive microtrauma, the development of symptomatic MDI represents a failure of compensation. [16] Many individuals with constitutional hyperlaxity remain asymptomatic throughout their lives because their dynamic stabilizers, the rotator cuff and periscapular muscles, provide sufficient neuromuscular control to keep the humeral head centered in the glenoid. [16] MDI becomes clinically manifest only when this dynamic control system is overwhelmed, fatigued, or uncoordinated and can no longer compensate for the deficient static restraints. This concept is central to understanding both the pathophysiology of MDI and the rationale for its primary treatment, which focuses on restoring this dynamic stability. [16] [17]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Epidemiology
content: The precise incidence and prevalence of MDI in the general population remain largely unknown. [8] [18] This is primarily due to the historical lack of a uniform definition and the variability in diagnostic criteria used across clinical studies. [8] [19] MDI typically presents in younger individuals, with a peak incidence in the second and third decades of life. [4] This becomes significantly less common in individuals who are 40 and older. [20] This age-related decline is attributed to the natural physiological stiffening of collagenous tissues and a decrease in overall tissue compliance that occurs with aging. [4]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Epidemiology
content: While MDI has been classically associated with a predilection for sedentary women with poor muscular development, this represents an incomplete demographic picture. [4] The condition is also highly prevalent among men and women athletes who participate in sports requiring significant overhead motion and shoulder flexibility. The demands of these sports can lead to acquired laxity, making this athletic population particularly susceptible to developing MDI. [18] [21]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Pathophysiology
content: The core pathophysiological feature of MDI is a fundamental imbalance between the static and dynamic stabilizing forces of the glenohumeral joint. [22] [23] The static restraints, primarily the capsuloligamentous complex, are pathologically lax, creating an excessively large capsular volume and allowing for supraphysiologic translation of the humeral head on the glenoid. [22] However, it is crucial to differentiate between asymptomatic joint laxity, a constitutional trait, and symptomatic instability, a pathological condition. [24] The transition from laxity to instability occurs when the dynamic stabilizers, including the rotator cuff and scapular muscles, cannot provide adequate compensatory stability, leading to symptoms such as pain, weakness, or a feeling of the shoulder "giving way" during activity. [22] [23]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Pathophysiology
content: Recent evidence suggests that the pathophysiology of MDI extends beyond the peripheral joint structures and involves a central nervous system component. [23] [25] Functional magnetic resonance imaging studies have shown altered brain activation patterns in patients with atraumatic instability during shoulder movements compared to healthy controls. [26] Clinically, this manifests as altered neuromuscular control, with electromyography studies revealing aberrant muscle activation patterns and impaired scapulothoracic and glenohumeral musculature coordination. [16] This suggests that MDI is not merely a condition of a "loose capsule" but rather a complex neuromuscular disorder where the brain's motor control strategies for stabilizing the shoulder are dysfunctional. [25] This understanding has profound implications for rehabilitation, which must focus on strengthening muscles and retraining these faulty motor patterns. [16]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- History and Physical
content: The clinical diagnosis of MDI is predicated on a thorough history and a detailed physical examination, as the condition often lacks a singular, dramatic inciting event.
contents: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- History and Physical. The clinical diagnosis of MDI is predicated on a thorough history and a detailed physical examination, as the condition often lacks a singular, dramatic inciting event.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- History and Physical -- History
content: Patients with MDI typically present with an insidious onset of vague, activity-related shoulder pain rather than a chief complaint of instability. [22] The pain is often described as a deep ache, exacerbated by overhead activities, lifting, or carrying heavy objects, which places inferior traction on the shoulder. [22] Many patients, particularly athletes, may report a decline in performance, a "dead arm" sensation, or a lack of strength and endurance during their sport. Essential inquiry regarding symptoms in the contralateral shoulder helps identify multidirectional instability that may be bilateral, particularly in individuals with underlying hyperlaxity. [18]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- History and Physical -- History
content: A critical history component is screening for voluntary or habitual instability. Patients who can intentionally and painlessly subluxate or dislocate their shoulder may have a significant underlying psychological component or be motivated by secondary gain. [27] As first described by Rowe et al, these individuals have been shown to have significantly poorer outcomes following surgical intervention, and their treatment plan must account for these psychosocial factors. [28]

content: The physical examination is the cornerstone of diagnosis. [29] The patient should be appropriately gowned to allow for visualization of both shoulders and the entire scapulothoracic region.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- History and Physical -- Inspection
content: Observe for any muscle atrophy, asymmetry, or scapular dyskinesis (abnormal positioning or motion of the scapula). [25]

content: Assess for tenderness over the glenohumeral joint lines and surrounding soft tissues.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- History and Physical -- Range of motion
content: The active and passive ranges of motion should be assessed and compared to the contralateral side. Patients with MDI often exhibit generalized or shoulder-specific hypermobility. [30]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- History and Physical -- Provocative testing
content: A series of tests is performed to assess for instability in multiple planes. Sulcus sign: This is the most consistent and characteristic physical finding in MDI. [27] Inferior traction is applied with the patient's arm in a neutral, adducted position. A positive test is the appearance of a visible and palpable sulcus or depression beneath the acromion. The sign is often graded based on the distance from the acromion to the humeral head (grade 1: <1 cm; grade 2: 12– cm; grade 3: >2 cm). [31] A sulcus of 2 cm or more, especially if it reproduces the patient's symptoms, highly suggests pathologic inferior laxity. [4] Load and shift test: This test assesses anterior and posterior translation. With the patient supine and the shoulder in various degrees of abduction, the examiner applies an axial load to the humerus to center it in the glenoid, and then translates the humeral head anteriorly and posteriorly. The amount of translation is graded and compared to the contralateral side. Apprehension and relocation tests: While classic for anterior instability, these tests can also be positive in MDI. [18] The apprehension test involves bringing the shoulder into 90° of abduction and maximal external rotation, which may elicit a sense of apprehension or impending subluxation. The relocation test confirms anterior instability, where a posteriorly directed force on the proximal humerus relieves the symptoms. [4]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- History and Physical -- Assessment for generalized hypermobility
content: Evaluating for systemic ligamentous laxity is a critical part of the workup. [24] The Beighton score, first described by Beighton and Horan in 1969 (see Table. The Beighton Score for Generalized Joint Hypermobility), is the most widely used clinical tool. [32]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- History and Physical
content: Acknowledging that the Beighton score serves as a screening tool for generalized laxity, rather than a definitive diagnostic test for shoulder pathology, is essential. [33] There is a demonstrated poor correlation between a patient's Beighton score and the degree of instrumented laxity specific to their shoulder. Therefore, a high score does not confirm MDI, and a low score does not exclude it. Other shoulder-specific laxity measures, such as passive external rotation of 85° or more with the arm adducted at the side, may provide more relevant information about the state of the glenohumeral joint's static restraints. [8] [19] The clinical picture must be synthesized from both general and shoulder-specific findings.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Evaluation
content: While MDI is primarily a clinical diagnosis, imaging is crucial in confirming the underlying pathology, ruling out other conditions, and guiding surgical planning when necessary. [4] [18]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Evaluation -- Radiographs and Computed Tomography
content: The initial imaging workup for suspected MDI includes a standard radiographic series of the shoulder, consisting of a true anteroposterior view in the scapular plane, a scapular-Y view, and an axillary lateral view. [18] In the majority of MDI cases, these radiographs are normal. [34] Their primary utility is to exclude other potential causes of shoulder pain and instability, such as significant glenoid bone loss (eg, a large bony Bankart lesion), glenoid dysplasia or hypoplasia, humeral head impaction fractures (Hill-Sachs lesions), or an os acromiale accessory ossicle. [34] Computed tomography is not routinely indicated for the initial diagnosis of MDI, but becomes invaluable for preoperative planning if there is suspicion of significant bony pathology. [35] [36] Computed tomography provides superior characterization and quantification of glenoid or humeral head bone loss, allowing for precise measurement of glenoid version, which can contribute to instability. [35]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Evaluation -- Magnetic Resonance Arthrography
content: Magnetic resonance arthrography (MRA) is the imaging modality of choice for evaluating the soft-tissue structures in MDI. [37] [38] The procedure involves injecting a dilute gadolinium-based contrast agent directly into the glenohumeral joint, which distends the joint capsule. [38] This capsular distension is critical, as it separates and clearly delineates the labrum, ligaments, and capsule, allowing for a much more sensitive and specific assessment than nonarthrographic magnetic resonance imaging. [37] The evolution of MRA has begun to shift the diagnosis of MDI from a purely subjective clinical assessment to one that is supported by objective, measurable data. [10] [27] The key findings on MRA in a patient with MDI can be organized by the anatomic structures involved, including capsular, rotator interval, labral, and ligamentous pathology.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Evaluation -- Capsular Pathology
content: The hallmark of MDI on MRA is evidence of a globally redundant and capacious joint capsule. [27] [39] This is most characteristically seen as a patulous inferior capsule and axillary recess, which appears as a large, U-shaped pouch rather than a taut, V-shaped structure. [40] This finding is the radiological correlate of a positive clinical sulcus sign. Beyond this qualitative assessment, quantitative metrics have been developed to objectify the diagnosis. The glenocapsular (GC) ratio, calculated by dividing the capsule's cross-sectional area by the glenoid's height on a coronal image, is a particularly useful tool. [40] [41] Results from a study found that a GC ratio greater than 1.42 demonstrated a sensitivity of 92.3% and a specificity of 89.2% for diagnosing MDI, providing a powerful, objective measure of inferior capsular redundancy. [40]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Evaluation -- Rotator Interval Pathology
content: The rotator interval, the space between the supraspinatus and subscapularis tendons containing the superior glenohumeral and coracohumeral ligaments, is frequently abnormal in MDI. [22] MRA can demonstrate widening of this interval, suggesting laxity of these important superior static restraints. [39]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Evaluation -- Associated Labral and Ligamentous Pathology
content: While MDI is primarily a disorder of capsular laxity, subtle or overt labral tears can coexist. [42] MRA is highly effective at identifying these lesions, which can include attenuation or fraying of the labrum, concealed tears such as a posteroinferior Kim lesion, or more extensive tears like SLAP (superior labrum anterior to posterior) lesions that may extend into the posterior labrum. [43] The glenohumeral ligaments may appear thinned, attenuated, or stripped from their insertions. [38] [44]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management
content: Treatment for individuals with MDI requires a nuanced approach that begins with recognizing the unique demands placed on the shoulder. Joint laxity may be a competitive advantage in some sports, making a standardized algorithm inappropriate. Instead, management is tailored to each patient’s goals, expectations, and functional needs. Given the complex interplay of capsular laxity, neuromuscular control, and individual factors, MDI remains challenging for clinicians and patients. Overall, the management of MDI is tailored to the individual patient, considering their symptoms, functional demands, and underlying etiology. [45] A structured, stepwise approach beginning with nonoperative management is the universally accepted standard of care. [16] [17]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management -- Overview
content: MDI commonly develops when the balance between dynamic and static stabilizers is disrupted. Accordingly, first-line treatment centers on physical therapy that targets strengthening the dynamic stabilizers of the shoulder, particularly the rotator cuff and periscapular musculature. Closed kinetic chain exercises are emphasized to retrain co-contraction and coordinated movement, thereby improving dynamic stability. Therapy should be extensive, lasting at least 3 to 6 months, before more aggressive interventions are considered. This approach is supported by the natural stiffening of the shoulder with age, as symptoms of MDI often decrease near skeletal maturity, making prolonged rehabilitation strongly recommended. [21] [46] [47] [48] [49] [50] [51]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management -- Overview
content: Rehabilitation alone is not always sufficient. Individuals with generalized hyperlaxity or entrenched maladaptive movement patterns may fail to respond to standard protocols. Recent literature highlights this complexity, suggesting that outcomes may hinge less on isolated muscle strengthening and more on how patients relearn coordinated shoulder control through movement retraining and feedback mechanisms. Hippensteel et al emphasize that rehabilitation success is closely tied to restoring neuromuscular control rather than simply targeting specific muscle groups. [1]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management -- Overview
content: Pain modulation strategies are gaining increasing recognition in managing multidirectional shoulder instability. Contemporary rehabilitation programs incorporate cognitive-behavioral principles and motor control retraining, particularly for individuals with chronic symptoms. The therapeutic emphasis extends beyond traditional strengthening exercises, focusing instead on restoring efficient, unguarded movement patterns through neuromuscular re-education and cognitive engagement. [52] Interestingly, there has been a recent push toward biological surgery. Various open vs arthroscopic stabilization procedures are described in the literature. Traditional open inferior capsular shift procedures are being replaced by arthroscopic capsular plication techniques, which are less invasive and preserve more motion.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management -- Overview
content: The documented long-term results of arthroscopic pancapsular shift show sustained functional improvement at 9-year follow-up. [19] Stabilization procedures include capsular shift, closure of the rotator interval, and plication of redundant capsular tissue. [53] Capsular allograft reconstruction, although uncommon, has also been described for those with collagen disorders. All glenoid or labrum pathology should be addressed at the same time if they are found to contribute to the patient’s instability. Several studies have explored procedures like posterior bone block augmentation and soft tissue reinforcement in hyperlax or congenital MDI cases.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management -- Overview
content: A 2024 case series by Di Francia et al employed arthroscopic subscapularis augmentation with a posterior bone block and reported more than 45% improvement in Constant scores (assessing shoulder function, strength, and range of motion) and American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons scores (evaluating pain and daily activity) at 1-year follow-up. [42] However, these findings are based on small series, and evidence that capsular plication consistently preserves full shoulder range of motion has not been reliably reproduced across multiple studies. A systematic review by Sahin et al acknowledged that these newer methods, although appealing, still lack long-term data. [54] Some patients, such as overhead athletes, reported subtle limitations in external rotation or difficulties returning to play.

content: Rehabilitation strategies are becoming more targeted, surgical techniques are refined, and classification systems are more thoughtful. However, each advancement brings new questions. Given the variability and patient-specific nature of MDI, a cautious and individualized approach remains essential. Innovation must be balanced with clinical judgment and adaptability.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management -- Nonsurgical Management
content: A comprehensive, supervised physical therapy program is the definitive first-line treatment for patients with MDI; this should be diligently pursued for a minimum of 3 to 6 months before considering surgical intervention. [3] While historical rehabilitation programs focused on generalized strengthening, modern protocols are based on a sophisticated understanding of the neuromuscular deficits in MDI. [22] The goal is not simply to build stronger muscles but to retrain the brain and nervous system to control unstable joints. [8] [16]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management -- Key principles of MDI rehabilitation
content: Scapular stabilization Correcting scapular dyskinesis is a foundational step. [22] [23] Exercises focus on strengthening the serratus anterior, rhomboids, and lower trapezius to provide a stable base for glenohumeral motion. [51]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management -- Key principles of MDI rehabilitation
content: Neuromuscular re-education and proprioception The program emphasizes restoring coordinated muscle activation patterns. [22] [23] This involves closed-chain exercises to promote co-contraction of the rotator cuff and deltoid and drills that challenge joint position sense. [22]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management -- Key principles of MDI rehabilitation
content: Phased and progressive approach Structured protocols, such as the Watson Instability Program, guide patients through specific stages of treatment. [51] The initial stages focus on establishing control of the scapular and humeral heads in low elevation ranges. Subsequent stages progressively introduce more complex, multi-planar, and functional movements, culminating in sport-specific or occupation-specific drills. [8] [16] [17] [51] The success of nonoperative management is variable. [10] [27] Many patients achieve significant and lasting symptom relief. [8] [16] However, long-term studies indicate that a substantial minority, particularly those with more severe laxity or higher functional demands, may ultimately fail conservative care and require surgery. [16] [17]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Management
content: Surgical intervention is reserved for patients with persistent, debilitating symptoms that have failed to improve despite a compliant and comprehensive trial of nonoperative management. [8] The fundamental goal of surgery is to reduce the pathologic capsular volume and restore appropriate tension to the static stabilizers, thereby eliminating symptomatic instability. [8] [55] The historical gold standard procedure was the open inferior capsular shift, which involved a subscapularis tenotomy to expose the joint. This was followed by incising and advancing the inferior capsule superiorly to tighten it. [1] [22] While effective, this procedure has mainly been supplanted by less invasive techniques.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Management
content: The current standard of care is arthroscopic pancapsular plication, also known as capsular shift. Performed through small portals, this technique allows the surgeon to systematically imbricate and suture the redundant capsular tissue from the joint's anterior, inferior, and posterior aspects, effectively tailoring the volume reduction to the patient's specific pattern of laxity. This approach avoids the morbidity of taking down the subscapularis tendon, allows for diagnosing and treating any coexisting intra-articular pathology (eg, labral tears), and is associated with a faster recovery. [55] [56] Long-term studies of arthroscopic pancapsular shift have demonstrated durable and significant improvements in patient-reported outcomes, with up to 82% at an 8-year follow-up. [19] Despite these excellent results, a notable portion of patients (approximately 29%) may report some residual feelings of instability, even if they are highly satisfied with their functional improvement and pain relief. [19]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management -- Emerging and Novel Treatment Strategies
content: For patients with recalcitrant MDI, particularly those with underlying connective tissue disorders or who have failed previous surgery, the future of treatment is moving beyond simply "tightening the capsule." Several novel strategies target different aspects of MDI's complex pathophysiology, heralding a future of more personalized and targeted interventions. [44]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management -- Biological augmentation (collagen cross-linking)
content: Targeting the material properties of the capsule itself, preclinical research is investigating the use of riboflavin and ultraviolet light to induce cross-linking within the collagen matrix of the capsule. This process has been shown to increase the biomechanical stiffness of the tissue significantly and may eventually offer a method to augment capsular integrity without surgical resection. [57]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management -- Neuromuscular modulation with electric muscle stimulation
content: The "shoulder pacemaker" concept utilizes neuromuscular electrical stimulation to retrain aberrant muscle firing patterns to address central neuromuscular control deficits. [58] A recent randomized controlled trial demonstrated that neuromuscular electrical stimulation-enhanced physical therapy was significantly more effective than physical therapy for patients with functional shoulder instability, suggesting a powerful new tool to augment rehabilitation. [47] [59]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Treatment / Management -- Advanced ligamentous and bony reconstruction
content: Advanced reconstructive options are being developed for the most severe and complex cases. Coracohumeral ligament reconstruction, using a tendon allograft or autograft, has been described as a salvage procedure for patients with a persistently incompetent rotator interval and inferior instability after failed primary surgery. [8] In rare instances of MDI associated with congenital glenoid hypoplasia or significant bone deficiency, bone-based augmentation procedures using bone blocks can be employed to enhance static stability by increasing the depth and surface area of the glenoid. [5] These emerging therapies represent a critical shift in the field. Rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all approach, future treatments evolve toward highly individualized strategies tailored to each patient’s specific pathology, whether rooted in tissue quality, neuromuscular control, or structural deficiency. [60]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Unidirectional instability Isolated anterior or posterior instability may have a more distinct traumatic onset and different physical exam findings. Cervical spine disease Cervical radiculopathy can refer pain to the shoulder and cause periscapular muscle weakness, mimicking the symptoms of MDI. A careful neurologic exam is essential. Thoracic outlet syndrome Compression of the brachial plexus or subclavian vessels can cause diffuse arm pain, weakness, and neurologic symptoms that can be confused with instability. Os acromiale A failure of the acromial ossification center to fuse can lead to painful motion and may be mistaken for an intra-articular process. Suprascapular neuropathy Entrapment of the suprascapular nerve can cause posterior shoulder pain and weakness of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. [1]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis for MDI is generally favorable, particularly for patients committed to a comprehensive rehabilitation program. [16] The symptoms of MDI are inversely proportional to the strength and neuromuscular control of the dynamic shoulder stabilizers; therefore, as strength and neuromuscular control improve, symptoms tend to resolve. [54] For patients who require surgery, modern arthroscopic techniques yield good to excellent results in most cases. However, outcomes are generally considered less predictable than those for surgery for traumatic, unidirectional instability. [55] Factors associated with a more guarded prognosis include the presence of a diagnosed connective tissue disorder, significant psychosocial comorbidities, and voluntary or habitual instability. [19]

content: Most complications associated with MDI are related to its surgical treatment. [61] While relatively uncommon, potential complications include:

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Complications
content: Postoperative stiffness Overtightening of the capsule during a plication procedure can result in a significant loss of motion, particularly in external rotation. This is the most common complication and can be challenging to manage. [62]
contents: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Complications. This is the most common complication and can be challenging to manage. [62]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Complications
content: Recurrence of instability Despite surgical tightening, some patients may experience a recurrence of their instability, particularly those with underlying collagen disorders or who return to high-demand activities prematurely. [63] Recurrence of instability was commonly seen following thermal capsulorrhaphy as it induced irreparable damage to the shoulder capsule. For this reason, thermal capsulorrhaphy has fallen out of favor and is now only mentioned for historical purposes. [64] [65]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Complications
content: Nerve injury The axillary nerve is at risk during dissection around the inferior aspect of the glenohumeral joint, particularly during open procedures. Injury can result in deltoid weakness and sensory loss.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Complications
content: Postcapsulorrhaphy arthritis Historically, overly aggressive tightening procedures were associated with increased joint reaction forces, leading to accelerated chondral wear and glenohumeral arthritis. [62] Capsulorrhaphy-induced arthritis was commonly seen following Magnuson-Stack or Putti-Platte procedures, which dramatically tightened the capsule and compressed the humeral head into the glenoid, effectively increasing the rate of cartilage degeneration. Modern, more anatomic techniques have reduced this risk.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Complications
content: Subscapularis deficiency This is a specific complication of open capsular shift procedures that require taking down and repairing the subscapularis tendon. Failure of the tendon to heal can lead to significant weakness and dysfunction. [62] This complication is avoided mainly with arthroscopic techniques.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: The postoperative rehabilitation protocol is as critical to a successful outcome as the surgery. [66] While specific protocols may vary, the general principles involve a phased progression to protect the surgical repair while gradually restoring motion, strength, and function. A typical timeline includes 4 to 6 weeks of shoulder immobilization in a sling for early capsular healing. [16] During this time, passive motion may be initiated under the guidance of a therapist, but abduction and external rotation are carefully limited, often to no more than 45°. [67]

[16] During this time, passive motion may be initiated under the guidance of a therapist, but abduction and external rotation are carefully limited, often to no more than 45°. [67]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: After 6 weeks, active-assisted and active range of motion are gradually increased. Gentle strengthening exercises typically begin around 12 to 16 weeks postoperatively. Returning to unrestricted activities and high-demand sports is usually prohibited until at least 6 months postoperatively. This is often delayed until 9 to 12 months, pending the restoration of strength, endurance, and neuromuscular control comparable to the contralateral shoulder for contact sports. [16] [50] [51] [54]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patient education is a fundamental component of successful MDI management. Setting realistic expectations from the outset is imperative. [68] Patients must understand that a lengthy and dedicated trial of physical therapy is the primary treatment and is often curative, which can help manage desires for a quick surgical fix. They should be educated on the inverse relationship between their symptoms and the functional capacity of their shoulder girdle musculature. [51] This understanding helps motivate long-term adherence to a maintenance exercise program, as symptoms will likely reappear if the shoulder becomes deconditioned. [50] Lifestyle and activity modifications may also be necessary to avoid positions and loads that cause symptoms.

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Key facts to keep in mind about MDI include: MDI is a complex neuromuscular condition, not just a simple case of a loose joint. Physical therapy focused on scapular stabilization and neuromuscular re-education is the cornerstone of treatment and must be exhausted before surgical intervention is considered. The TUBS/AMBRI classification is obsolete. A modern diagnostic approach should separately consider the roles of trauma and generalized hyperlaxity. [8] Magnetic resonance arthrography is the gold standard for imaging, with quantitative measures, such as the glenocapsular ratio, providing objective evidence of capsular pathology. Arthroscopic pancapsular plication is the current surgical standard of care, offering durable long-term results. Clinicians must maintain a high index of suspicion for voluntary or habitual instability, as these patients often have underlying psychological factors and are poor candidates for surgery. [11] [16] [23] [28]

title: Multidirectional Shoulder Instability -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The successful management of MDI requires a highly integrated and collaborative approach. [69] Due to the complex nature of the diagnosis and the long-term commitment necessary for successful treatment, effective communication between the orthopedic surgeon, physical therapists, and the patient is paramount. The surgeon is responsible for establishing an accurate diagnosis and ruling out other pathologies, while the physical therapist designs and implements the specialized, progressive rehabilitation program. The patient's active participation and "buy-in" to the lengthy treatment plan are critical for a successful outcome. A strong, communicative healthcare team can enhance patient compliance, optimize functional recovery, and improve patient satisfaction and long-term results.
